title: Many chains
hookLine: some reports come through so many chains that they're certain

cards: Have you ever stood in Antarctica? If not, can you prove it's there? Not with your own eyes.
And yet nobody lies awake wondering whether it was invented. Explorers, scientists, maps, photographs, people with no reason to agree with each other, all saying the same thing.

At some point, doubting it would take more effort than believing it. Muslim scholars of law and hadith used this kind of example, a far-off place you've never visited, to explain a special kind of knowing.
Not a report from one person. A report from so many that it can't be a lie. Today, mutawatir.

teach.b: A mutawatir report is carried by so many people, at every step of its chain, that their agreeing on a falsehood is beyond belief. Not one chain: many, running side by side, from the first generation down.
How many is so many? Here scholars differ, and say so. Some proposed a minimum number.
Others said no fixed number works: the crowd has to be large and varied enough that knowledge follows without effort, the way it does about that faraway place.
An example scholars give: the Prophet ﷺ said, in a report in both Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, whoever tells a lie about me on purpose, let him take his seat in the Fire.
Scholars describe that sentence as reaching them through companion after companion, by many roads.
Notice the irony: a report carried this widely is a warning against inventing reports. Now the contrast.

teach.h: AHAD: ONE CHAIN, OR A FEW.
teach.b: Plenty of reports come through one chain, or a few, and scholars call them ahad, solitary. That's not an insult. A solitary report can be sound, and acted on.
But scholars of theology and law have discussed what kind of knowledge a single chain gives, and they don't all answer the same way.

And something bigger: Muslim scholars describe the Qur'an itself as carried this way, recited aloud by crowds in every generation, not passed down a single line. So certainty, in this science, isn't a feeling.
It's a crowd that couldn't all have made it up.

how: Scholars of hadith and legal theory distinguish mutawatir reports, carried by so many that they give certainty, from ahad reports carried by one or a few chains, and Muslims describe the Qur'an as transmitted by mass recitation in every generation.

games.q: you've never been to a far-off city, but travelers from everywhere, strangers to each other, describe it the same way. what do the scholars say you have?
games.why: a crowd that couldn't all have agreed on a lie gives certain knowledge. that's the idea behind mutawatir.

practice: Name three things you're sure of: one you saw yourself, one a single person told you, and one so many people said, from so many directions, that you've never thought to doubt it.
Hold each up in turn and ask how you know it, which feels solid, and which feels solid but is really one voice. Don't rush to change your mind about anything; just sort them.

wordCard.voice: Mutawatir. A report carried by so many, through so many chains, that it gives certain knowledge. It ends a week that walked through hadith, sunnah, isnad, matn and sahih. Today's word.
